title: Unsorted Columns in a Word Grid
statement:
You get n lowercase strings strs, all of the same length. Write them one under another to form a grid of letters: row i is strs[i].

A column is sorted when its letters, read top to bottom, never go down in the alphabet. Equal neighbours are fine. Return how many columns are not sorted.

examples.why: Column 0 reads b, c, d (sorted). Column 1 reads a, o, i and column 2 reads t, w, g; both drop somewhere.
Only column 0 (z, y, x) is out of order. Column 1 is a, a, a: equal letters count as sorted.
Every column goes up from top to bottom.

constraints: All strings have the same length
hints: Each column can be judged on its own. What makes a single column fail?
A column is unsorted as soon as one letter is larger than the letter directly below it.
Loop over columns on the outside and rows on the inside; stop checking a column at its first drop.

explain.intuition:
A sequence is non-decreasing exactly when every adjacent pair is in order. So a column is unsorted the moment you find a row i with strs[i][col] > strs[i + 1][col]. You never need to sort anything or compare letters that are far apart.

Put the column loop outside and the row loop inside, so you can stop at the first drop and move to the next column.
steps: For each column c, walk rows i from 0 to n − 2.
If strs[i][c] > strs[i + 1][c], add 1 to count and stop this column.
pitfalls: Treating equal letters as a drop. a, a, a is sorted.
Checking only the first and last letter of a column: a, c, b starts low and ends high but is still unsorted.
Counting every drop instead of every column, so a column with two drops is counted twice.

solutions.title: Compare each column with its sorted copy
solutions.idea: Read each column into a string, sort it, and count the columns that changed.

solutions.title: Look for one drop per column
solutions.idea: A column is unsorted exactly when some letter is larger than the one below it.

followups: Instead of each column on its own, delete the fewest columns so that the rows, read as whole strings, end up in sorted order.
The strings arrive one at a time as a stream. Keep the count up to date after each new row.
